extracted.intended_audience: educated correspondents, political actors, and friends of Benjamin Franklin (18th‑century public/intellectual readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of Benjamin Franklin's letters containing prescriptive guidance for moral/prudential decision‑making and for composing and handling correspondence and diplomatic propositions. Emphasis is on how to weigh reasons, write clear requests, and conduct/openly present political negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral or prudential algebra (pro/con balancing method)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a difficult case presents conflicting reasons, divide a sheet into two columns labelled 'pro' and 'con', jot short hints of motives as they occur over several days, then estimate their respective weights and eliminate equal weights until where the balance lies is evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write reasons for and against over three or four days so all occurences appear together; when you find causes equal on opposite sides, strike them both out; if one pro equals two cons, strike the three, etc. Though weights aren't algebraic exact, considering each separately and comparatively reduces rash decisions and yields better judgment ('prudential algebra').

rubrics_metrics.name: Letter writing to strangers — three essential points
rubrics_metrics.description: A stranger writing to request assistance should: (1) propose something practicable; (2) make propositions in explicit terms so they are easily understood; (3) ask for what is in itself reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure in any of these makes the correspondent appear negligent and makes it proper to withhold encouragement or answer. Clear, practicable, and reasonable requests create a favorable impression and invite further acquaintance or assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require specificity to judge requests (avoid vague phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests expressed in vague or relative terms (e.g., 'without too great expense' or 'to be received in a suitable manner') are not answerable because the recipient cannot judge feasibility or reasonableness without concrete particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When replying or deciding on assistance, demand concrete details about costs, expectations, and definitions of terms so the correspondent's capacity and the request's reasonableness can be assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not give letters of recommendation for unknown persons
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not provide letters of recommendation for people whose character and qualifications one does not personally know, because such indiscriminate recommendations undermine the recommender's authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refuse or withhold endorsements for correspondents known only by name and place; a recommender whose endorsements are given without knowledge will lose credibility and the value of future recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomatic/propositional openness — use official, frank channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Those seeking to negotiate peace or similar political arrangements should propose openly to the authorized body (e.g., Congress) fair and equal terms rather than seeking secret or mysterious private correspondences or intermediaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret proposals or clandestine exchanges while formal commissioners or treaties are in place are improper, presumptuous, and may have mischievous consequences. Open, direct offers through proper authorities better serve negotiation and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid engaging in or acting on private/insidious conciliatory schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Private flattering approaches, promises of places, pensions, or honours intended to induce betrayal or capitulation should be treated with suspicion as attempts at corruption or court intrigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View offers of offices, pensions, or peerages as potential bribes; consider their origins and practicalities (e.g., whether such places would even exist or be paid for locally) before treating them as bona fide inducements. Such offers can indicate ulterior motives and render the offeror untrustworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not encourage or promise assistance beyond your authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not encourage volunteers or applicants to undertake actions (e.g., joining an army) when you have no authority or orders to place or support them; giving encouragement without capacity to follow through is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be candid about the limits of your power; to avoid false expectations, decline to give assurances or to recommend placements you cannot actually secure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peaceable settlement of disputes as a public aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations (and people) ought to pursue plans to settle disputes without resorting to war; moral and practical efforts should be made to induce disputes' resolution peacefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin expresses a desire for discovery or institutions that induce nations to settle disputes without violence; as a rule, attempts to prevent war by honest and faithful action are morally and politically preferable and form the basis for later stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public advice/messaging: present frugality and industry as honorable motives
rubrics_metrics.description: If citizens adopt resolutions of frugality and industry (as in Boston), frame the motive as enabling faster and more effective discharge of debts to the mother country — this rhetoric softens measures and appears honorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When promoting austerity or reform to an external audience, present practical, honorable rationales (e.g., debt repayment) to reduce friction and improve appearance toward the other party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical personal conduct guidance (temper, economy, and self-reliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal improvement prescriptions include remedying 'ennui' by temperance, work (e.g., manual labor), and economy; a single woman, Franklin suggests, may live comfortably with economy on modest means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice is given as concrete behavioral prescriptions (e.g., a month in Bridewell to cure idleness, dismissing hairdressers to economize); these are framed as practical steps to improve health, spirits, and social contentment rather than abstract exhortations.
